claims.text: The target systems are multicomponent, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys with five or more principal elements.
The proposed intervention is to replace the EAM reference in TOR-TILD with a machine-learned interatomic potential.
The MLIP should be trained on diverse ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid phases.
MLIPs can include moment tensor potentials and deep neural-network potentials.
Traditional EAM references inadequately represent the many atomic configurations of ab initio high-entropy-alloy liquids.
EAM has a limited, predefined functional form and limited reference data.
A solid-and-liquid-trained MLIP will better reproduce the potential-energy surface across the broad configurational space of a high-entropy system.
Many-body interactions are critical in the disordered liquid state and can be captured adaptively by an MLIP.
Training on configurations from both phases will improve reference–target phase-space overlap near melting.
Improved phase-space overlap will produce a smoother and more representative thermodynamic-integration path.
The MLIP reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch and free-energy errors relative to TOR-TILD using EAM references.
The expected improvement in solid and liquid free-energy estimates will be nontrivial and measurable.
The method is intended to apply to equimolar or near-equimolar alloys with five or more components at or near their melting temperatures.
Configuration choice can produce measurable variation in simulated solid–liquid and liquid–solid transition temperatures in a multicomponent high-entropy material.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can generate ensembles of finite-temperature atomic configurations.
Elemental and binary calculations provide supporting evidence that the proposed MLIP reference will improve free-energy integration.
The exact magnitude of the free-energy-error reduction is uncertain without calibration on representative high-entropy alloys.

A decisive benchmark can compare EAM- and MLIP-referenced calculations of solid–liquid free-energy differences, integration-path mismatch, and predicted melting temperatures for the same alloy and conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in path mismatch, with MLIP errors comparable to or larger than EAM errors, would falsify the hypothesis.
